opus-5.5.text:
I think the spirit of ARC, as François laid it out, is really about skill-acquisition efficiency. It's not "can you get the right output grid," it's "can you pick up a genuinely new abstraction from a handful of examples, using only fairly generic prior knowledge." So when I look at an approach, the question I ask is less about the score and more about where the generalization is actually coming from.

A few things I look at concretely. First, how much of the solution was smuggled in by the designer. If someone hand-writes a domain-specific language that happens to have a primitive for exactly the kind of transformation the test tasks use, then the system isn't really discovering the abstraction, the human did. That's not worthless, but it's a different claim. Second, how the system behaves on things that are truly out of distribution relative to what it was trained or engineered on. ARC's hidden test set is supposed to be novel, and the interesting question is whether your method degrades gracefully there or just falls off a cliff.

Third, and this one's a bit more subtle, I care about whether the approach produces something like an explanation. In our work with program synthesis, and more recently with combining language models and program search, part of the appeal is that you get an explicit hypothesis, a program, that you can check against the examples. That feels closer to what a person does: you form a theory of the puzzle, you verify it, you revise. A big transductive model that just emits a grid can also work surprisingly well, and actually we found induction and transduction are pretty complementary, they solve different kinds of problems. But I'd say the spirit is better served when you can point to the mechanism and say: this is the generalization, here's why it holds.

And honestly, I try not to be too purist about it. Compute and pretraining data both matter, and I don't think using a large pretrained model automatically violates the spirit, since humans come in with a lot of priors too. The real question is whether the priors are general, things like objects, counting, symmetry, goal-directedness, or whether they're narrowly tuned to the benchmark. If it's the latter, you've built an ARC solver. If it's the former, you might have learned something about intelligence.

r001.rationale: It says a hand-written DSL with primitives tailored to ARC test transformations means the human supplied the abstraction, moving the approach away from the intended claim.

r002.rationale: It contrasts general priors with benchmark-tuned ones, but does not raise the unresolved question of how much ARC-specific specialization is necessary to solve ARC.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute to Chollet the belief that the ARC dataset alone contains sufficient information to solve ARC.

r004.rationale: It discusses generalization to ARC's hidden test set, but does not propose success on related problems beyond ARC as a way to discourage human-encoded hacks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that there are two different questions tangled together there, and you have to pull them apart. One is whether a system scores well on ARC, and the other is whether it does so for the reasons François cared about when he built it. Those can come apart, and the whole history of benchmarks tells you they will come apart if you let them.

So the test I apply is roughly this. ARC was designed to measure something like skill acquisition efficiency. The puzzles are meant to be novel, so the question is: given a tiny handful of examples, can you figure out the rule and apply it? If an approach gets its mileage by having seen hundreds of thousands of synthetic ARC-like tasks, and then recognizes the test tasks as near neighbors of things it's already seen, that's a very different claim about intelligence than a system that walks in with only core knowledge priors, the stuff a child has, and genuinely infers the rule on the spot. Both might score the same. One captures the spirit and the other sort of evades it.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I don't think that means pretraining or data augmentation is cheating. Humans don't come to ARC blank either. We've had years of experience with objects, counting, symmetry, occlusion. So the question isn't "did you use prior experience," it's "what is the ratio of prior experience to what you're able to do with it." That's the efficiency framing, and I find it much more useful than a purity test.

A couple of concrete signals I look at. First, does the method have a genuine notion of a hypothesis, something you can inspect and that is either right or wrong about the task? Program synthesis approaches, which is where a lot of my own work has been, have that property almost by construction. You can show me the program. Neural approaches increasingly have something analogous if you look at test-time training or at models that write out natural language descriptions of the rule before they predict. If there's no hypothesis anywhere, just pattern completion straight to output pixels, I get nervous, because I can't tell whether it understood the task or just interpolated.

Second, how does it behave off-distribution? Take a method that does well and probe it with tasks constructed to be genuinely unlike the training distribution. The spirit of ARC lives in the gap between performance on familiar-looking tasks and performance on unfamiliar ones. If that gap is enormous, the system has learned ARC-the-dataset rather than ARC-the-problem.

And third, honestly, I ask whether the approach teaches us anything. The reason ARC is interesting isn't the leaderboard. It's that it's one of the few places where you can study few-shot inductive reasoning in a controlled way. If a method cracks it and we come away with a clearer picture of how to combine search, learning, and compositional abstraction, then it captured the spirit regardless of the exact architecture. If it cracks it and we learn nothing except that scale works, that's a result, but it's a less satisfying one, and I suspect François would say the same.

r001.rationale: The response discusses synthetic ARC-like training and pattern completion, but does not say that designing an ARC-specific language moves an approach away from the benchmark’s intended spirit.

r002.rationale: It asks about the balance between prior experience and what a system can do with it, but does not raise the unresolved question of how much ARC-specific specialization is necessary.

r003.rationale: The response says ARC tasks require inferring rules from examples and mentions core knowledge priors; it does not attribute to Chollet the belief that the dataset alone contains sufficient information.

r004.rationale: It proposes testing on tasks unlike the training distribution, but does not propose success on related problems beyond ARC as a way to deter human-encoded ARC-specific hacks.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: where does the intelligence in the solution come from? Is the system actually looking at those few examples and figuring out a new rule, or have its designers already anticipated that kind of problem and built the solution into it?

Of course, you can’t avoid prior knowledge altogether. Even the choice of a representation gives you a bias. So I wouldn’t say that using search, or having a library of concepts, is somehow against the spirit of ARC. What matters is whether those concepts can be combined in genuinely new ways, and whether the system can infer the right combination from very little data.

The evidence I’d want is that you can freeze the system, give it new tasks that weren’t available to the people developing it, and it still adapts. The score matters, but so does what you had to put into the system to get that score. To me, the spirit is about acquiring a new capability from a few examples, rather than demonstrating a capability that was effectively supplied in advance.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether designers have built a solution in advance, but does not state that an ARC-specific domain language moves an approach away from ARC’s intended spirit.

r002.rationale: It acknowledges that prior knowledge and representation bias are unavoidable, but does not raise how much ARC-specific specialization is necessary to solve ARC.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute to François Chollet a belief that the ARC dataset alone contains sufficient information.

r004.rationale: It calls for testing on new tasks unavailable to developers, but does not propose success on related problems beyond ARC to discourage ARC-specific hacks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between doing well on the benchmark and demonstrating the kind of intelligence the benchmark is meant to measure. My understanding of François’s goal is that you should be able to look at a few examples, infer a new concept, and apply it to a new situation. So the question is: where is the work happening? Is the system actually constructing an explanation from those examples, or has the designer already supplied something very close to the solution?

But there isn’t a completely clean boundary, because every system has prior knowledge. Even choosing a programming language for a program synthesis system gives it a particular set of concepts. I’d want to make those assumptions explicit, and then ask whether the system can combine them in genuinely new ways. Success on held-out tasks is evidence, but I’d find it much more convincing if the same machinery could learn new abstractions and transfer them beyond the particular benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether designers have supplied something close to the solution, but does not mention a domain-specific language tailored to ARC or say that designing one moves away from ARC’s intended spirit.

r002.rationale: It says there is no clean boundary because systems have prior knowledge, but does not raise how much ARC-specific specialization is necessary to solve ARC.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute to Chollet a belief that the ARC dataset alone contains sufficient information to solve ARC.

r004.rationale: It says transfer beyond the benchmark would make success more convincing, but does not propose requiring success on related problems beyond ARC as a way to discourage human-encoded ARC-specific hacks.
